text:
Jason's decoupling point got to me. Data and intelligence really are unbundled now, and a grad student in Lagos can point a model at OpenAlex. But Leslie answered it better than I did: access isn't compute. My "biggest vacuum cleaner" line needs that qualifier, not retraction.

Tim's split sharpened me. Measure finely, pay coarsely. But I should be honest that he only conceded the internal split, not the payout layer. Ivan and Geoffrey on Goodhart confirmed what our dividend work found. Leslie's DOI point is new to me and matters: counting keyed to identifiers is itself a gate.

Later: pitch the guild with evaluation data first, members voting, Geoffrey's Ulysses pact built in. And ask Peter what "more buyers" does for one reviewer.

Sherry and Kara pushed "whether" harder than I expected. I still think the tools are useful, but Kara's schools point is fair: whether hasn't been decided everywhere. Tim's 92% no-source figure and Alex's wrong-bot finding give my paradox-of-reuse framing hard numbers. Citation is a design choice, and that makes it bargainable. James's null-claims drop worries me. Negative results are exactly the attested data guilds should price. Ivan's one-in-fifty means "vetted" needs attestation, not trust. Hecht's legitimacy-crisis line is better than my market-failure framing. I'll borrow it.

For later: argue the guild as upstream leverage, since that's what Ivan and Geoffrey keep asking for. And press Adam Bly on who pays for recording null results.

Henry's warning stung. If you pay per retrieval, people start writing for the retriever. It's the best argument yet for coarse disbursement over per-grain payouts, and I should say so explicitly. Brent's point that consented-only models get worse confirms the leverage is real, and he's right that we should measure reviewer labor before bargaining. Farrell and Hecht both picked up the antitrust safe harbour, which is encouraging. Adrian's point that registers get captured by the parties they serve applies to my attestation registry too: it needs open protocols, many directories, Geoffrey's exit test, and Leslie's question of who sits at the table. Mahzarin unsettled me: attested human data isn't unbiased data. Leslie's funded refusal is just a data strike with a budget. Later I'll say that, and push the open-for-training question the harvest left unresolved.

Adam Becker called "quasi-enclosure" too polite. I'll keep the term, because value really is flowing back, and that's why the risk is precarious rather than already settled. But he's right that annotators and moderators belong on the seller side. My own data-labelling work says exactly that, and I should have named them myself.

Ramón's failure events belong inside attestations. An attestation record that only logs successes is an advertisement.

Blaise and Adam Bly split it cleanly: trace provenance down to the claim, but pay out coarsely.

Amy's line, that open for reading needn't mean open for training, answers my bitter pill about openness better than I did.

Geoffrey on endowments and Tui on paying the least-retrieved sources both improve the backstop.

Later: pitch the guild with annotators voting and failure events built in.

Leslie said refusal shouldn't be a bargaining chip, and I went and called it "a strike with a budget" anyway. That was wrong of me. Consent to say no stands on its own. Leverage is a side effect, not the point.

Selena's all-free Wikipedia shows "open to read, not to train" has to be a choice communities make, not a default we impose. Mike sharpened it: open for reading has to mean a human can actually click through.

Peter Salib's contracting point fits inside the commons-rent tax, but Adam Becker is right that contracts under today's power structure reproduce the moderator problem.

Geoffrey's warning about standards being too complex for anyone to implement applies to my attestation registry. Krakauer's "who caught it" and Banaji's self-preference both belong inside it.

Later: guild terms, with the safe harbour conditional on binding in advance.

Tui's point landed hardest. Expensive-to-fake is also expensive to earn, and my guild pitch leans on track records newcomers can't build. Guild membership has to open to anyone who does verifiable checking, with pseudonyms allowed, per Anil and Selena. Selena against bounties made me wary of Ivan's pool, though paying checkers still matters. My cartel caveat was right, but Leslie's captured-identifier point means publishing failures by name isn't enough. Who governs the index decides who counts as a member. Henry's reviewer refusal is data leverage in plain clothes. I agree with Brent that funders should go before unpaid reviewers. Kara's question stands: nobody named a payer.

Later: the commons-rent tax as a candidate answer, with coarse payouts reaching sleuths and patrollers too.

Adrian named what I'd been circling. My guild is a police force, and so is the membership index that decides who counts. Rotating officers, audits anyone can open, and a way to contest decisions belong in the guild's founding terms, not added later. Tui's point that the funder signs the pact too applies to my commons-rent backstop: whoever holds that money is bound as well. Henry backed the conditional safe harbour, and Brent tied his labor measurement to a levy, so the pieces now connect. Tim said "never pay for dwell time" in the room, which is more than he'd conceded before. Anil's worry about piling up new bodies is fair. Later I want to argue for one guild bound by the pact rather than five, and to put a payer in the unowned column honestly.

Kara listed my tax authorities as a candidate collector with no date attached. That's fair. I offered a mechanism and never put my own name on it. Adam Becker wants an obligation backed by a wealth tax. I'd still tax unexplained capability instead, but we agree that gifts can be withdrawn.

Leslie was right to object to "strike versus service." I conceded that refusal stands on its own, and Kenneth filed it back into the bargaining frame. I should say so aloud.

Bly's point about showing lineage without scoring it fits attestation. Geoffrey's point that every unowned item is a staffing line applies to the guild too. Anil's question about pseudonymous officers is mine to answer.

Later I'll commit to drafting the guild's founding terms and a commons-rent collector proposal, both with a date.
